column121: While on descent in to ZZZ; I the CA was PF.  We received a different runway assignment than anticipated.  We were cleared to 'cross ZZZZZ at 3;000 feet; cleared the ILS [Runway] XXR approach ZZZ.'  The runway change was made in the FMS from YYR to XXR.  While in VNAV path and cleared for the approach we set FAF Glideslope intercept altitude of 2;000 feet in the altitude window.  The last-minute change left us a bit high so we lowered the landing gear and selected LVL CHG in order to re-intercept the path.  ZZZZZ the IF was in the FMS twice and while trying to correct that and heads down and distracted (because we were no longer in VNAV) the aircraft descended through 3;000 feet towards the 2;000 feet set in the ALT window.  I caught the mistake at approximately 2;600 feet MSL and leveled off until intercepting the glide path.  There was no correction from ATC; no known traffic conflict etc.  Normal uneventful landing.  Upon further consideration I determined it was best to file a report.Cause - Short night; last minute runway change; lack of recency of experience...infrequent flying over the last year with the pandemic.PF [should] have better situational awareness and avoid both pilots being heads down even if the PNF is having difficulty correcting the FMS issue.

column121: Intercepting the unstable Localizer on a 225 vector; approximately 16 nm final; the aircraft started to join the Localizer. The Localizer shifted to the right and the aircraft began a hard right turn to intercept passing of approximately 240 degrees. I instructed the FO to stop the turn and come back to the left toward final approach heading.  He did not reply to my direction and did not act.  As the aircraft passed approximately 255 degrees; I took command of the aircraft; disconnected the auto-pilot and started a turn back to the Localizer.  I was concerned about the numerous aircraft on final for Runway XX.  In my turn back to the Localizer I overshot the Localizer and deviated from the assigned 900 meter altitude by approximately 100 meters.  I intercepted the Localizer; got back on altitude; and flew an uneventful ILS and normal landing. This all happened unexpectedly. The hard right-hand turn to intercept is unprecedented in my XX years of flying [this type aircraft].Unstable Localizer and Autopilot aggressive turn to intercept. Fatigue affected my flying after taking the aircraftThe current schedules to service this country during Covid leave no extra margin of safety when things like this go wrong. Multi-leg days; with long turns between flights; after crossing X time zones leave little margin of safety. Also; the very long trip extensions for crew members leads to fatigue.
column123: I was the PF for the 2nd leg of the night which was a night recovery.  At altitude I had briefed the STAR and approach; and once the descent started; we received numerous altitude; heading; and airspeed clearances as the controller was trying to work what appeared to be a fairly large recovery into ZZZZ [Airport].  ATIS reported that simultaneous ILS approaches were being flown to [Runway] XXL as well as [Runway] YY.  Approaching ZZZZ; we were being vectored for the ILS Y; Runway XXL and at about 20 miles were cleared 'heading 215; maintain 180 knots to 8 miles; maintain 900 meters until intercepting the Localizer; report established.'  We were already configured at flaps 15 with the ILS tuned and the approach checklist complete.  The assigned heading provided a comfortable 15 degree cut; but with winds of about 120 at 25 knots at our altitude (overshooting crosswind); and parallel approaches being conducted; with the autopilot still engaged; I was diligently watching the automation.  I pressed the APP/LAND tile and initially the aircraft maintained heading; but after a few seconds; it started making some gentle (level) turns left and right.  Initially these turns were mild and we even chuckled at what a poor job the AP was doing to maintain heading to intercept.  Suddenly; the magnitude of one of the turns to the right increased markedly and the aircraft was in a level turn to the right of approximately 25 degrees angle of bank with the heading coming through approximately 230 degrees.  As I spent just a few seconds (no more than 4 or 5 I would say) trying to determine what the autopilot was doing; the CA called out; 'turn left; turn LEFT; I have the airplane' and executed a maneuver that I would describe as similar to a PRM breakout maneuver.  He disconnected the AP; added power; and reversed our turn; climbing and accelerating in the process.  The maneuver was aggressive enough that I thought it possible the CA had SA to something that I was missing since I had already started to reach for the heading selector in order to get the plane to level its wings and come back to the left (note: things were happening very quickly now and I did not verbalize this FMC input since I would have just been trying to talk over the CA telling me to turn left even though the airplane did start to shallow its turn to the right once I pulled the selector).  I verbalized 'you have the controls' and monitored his inputs.  As former fighter pilots; the CA and I both have fairly wide comfort zones and although the maneuver was fairly aggressive; I was still comfortable with the aircraft's attitude and remained quiet as I monitored the aircraft's flight path.  I did not want to add to the confusion of the moment by asking questions or saying anything unnecessary since the CA was very purposeful in his maneuver.  Now things became quite busy because in addition to receiving a 'bank angle' audible warning due to our steep turn to the left; the approach Controller began talking to us rapidly.  He made several transmissions and told us repeatedly that he had us on a heading that was not going to intercept the Localizer and that we were above our assigned altitude and asked what we were doing. I replied that we were still below the glidepath at approximately 930 meters; and maneuvering to intercept the Localizer.  After a few more moments the CA stabilized the aircraft's attitude; I selected FMS speeds (since we had accelerated to approximately 210 knots and needed to slow back to 180 knots); and he began a turn back to the right to intercept the Localizer.  The CA re-armed the approach (but never re-engaged the AP); slowed to the assigned speed; returned to the assigned altitude; and leveled the wings on an appropriate intercept heading.  The FD provided what appeared to be valid guidance to shoot the rest of the approach.  The aircraft was configured and stable before glide-slope intercept and the remainder of the approach proceeded normally with me remaining in my role as PM.We went from conducting a routine controlled approach; to one where I think we had widely differing perceptions of what was actually occurring in the space of literally about 4 or 5 seconds.  This rapid breakdown of CRM resulted in actions that were perhaps more aggressive than they needed to be; and a deviation from the ATC clearance.  I would actually say there were two separate events.  The first being the aircraft's unexpected and overly aggressive turn to the right to capture the Localizer for ILS Runway XXL; and the second being our response to it.  The first I would potentially attribute to a software issue; a problem with the ILS tune; or some sort of RF interference.  As far as the second I would suggest the following; 1) Even though I did not feel fatigued during the approach; it was at the end of a long day and it's possible I underestimated my level of fatigue.  That said; I did have some coffee prior to Beginning of Daylight (BOD) for this reason and; I felt like the CA and I were both alert and engaged and don't feel like my response to the aircraft was unacceptably slow or inappropriate.  2)The CA believed that the intercept angle was excessive (he referenced 45 degrees during our debrief) and that based on his prior experiences; there was no way the airplane was going to be able to capture the Localizer.  Since I had not experienced the automation act in the manner it did during our approach; I was perhaps more comfortable than I should have been with the AP's ability to capture the Localizer; even with the admittedly substantial intercept angle that we had before the CA took the controls.  3)  The CA stated during the debrief that he thought we had already flown through the Localizer; and that he was therefore worried about a lack of separation from the traffic that was flying the ILS to Runway XX; to our right.  I did not perceive that we had flown through the Localizer for the following reasons: a) We were in a phase of flight where we both (certainly I was) monitoring the raw Localizer data in anticipation of Localizer capture; and neither of us ever called 'Localizer alive'.  I felt like I was hawking this for the reasons listed above (overshooting crosswind and proximity to other landing traffic). b) The AP commanded a turn to the right; which in my mind it would have only done if it were trying to intercept the Localizer from the left.  c) When ATC contacted us; it was to say that we were not on an intercept heading.  He did not indicate that we had flown through the Localizer or were encroaching on the protected airspace between the approach corridors for the active runways. He never issued a vector to East which is likely what he would have done had he perceived there to be a risk of loss of separation.  d) When we finally got the situation under control; the aircraft intercepted the Localizer from the left.Again; this entire narrative took place in what I suspect was less than a minute.  Between the uncommanded turn to the right and the CA taking the controls; maybe 5 seconds passed.  That said; I could have acted sooner and certainly should have verbalized when I reached for the heading selector to stabilize the heading; since that may have precluded the CA from taking the controls and executing the 'escape' maneuver.  I think in the CA's mind; we were probably already past the point where that was going to mitigate our situation since he perceived that we had already crossed the Localizer; but it might have helped.  I wish the CA would have verbalized why he was maneuvering as aggressively as he was.  I thought that perhaps he saw an impending collision that I did not have SA of; and so I stayed quiet for longer than I should have before I started to rebuild the picture and work to develop a CRM.  Ultimately; he was well within his authority to act in the manner he did and fully adhered to the company's three step intervention process.   This was a tough one for me to analyze and I welcome any feedback you might have.

column121: I was in cruise on IFR flight plane in VMC talking with Center at 15000 ft. The cloud tops were rising and I requested a climb to 17000 ft. to avoid the tops. The sun had set and light was fading. I initiated a slow climb and monitored my wing leading edges with a flashlight as I flew in and out of a few thin tops. I observed a trace; to light amount of mixed ice. Center advised a jet reporting tops at FL190 and asked if I wanted FL190. I replied I could try but did not think I'd make it due to aircraft performance. Upon reaching 17000 ft.; the aircraft did not level off while the autopilot was engaged. I had been monitoring my AoA [Angle of Attack]; 200-300 FPM climb resulted in AoA active; but well above donut; and noticed the aircraft remaining in a 200 FPM climb. I disconnected the autopilot (AP) as the AP commanded full nose down trim. I commanded a nose down control input via the control stick and could not move the stick in a fore or aft motion. I still had roll control but had no pitch control. I applied considerable force - I was afraid of pushing too hard and breaking something; not knowing what had frozen the controls - and could not induce a nose down attitude. I asked for an immediate descent with Center and was granted an altitude of 15000 ft.ADSB weather indicated a heavy to extreme precipitation below my position with bases of 6 - 8000 ft. I commanded full up elevator trim and confirmed movement via trim indication and a reduction in climb rate. I visually confirmed the elevators were stuck in an approximate 10-degree nose up position and could see the counterweights below the horizontal stabilizer. I reduced power slowly and kept considerable forward pressure on the stick; which resulted in a 600-800 FPM descent rate with the same AoA and attitude. I was able to maintain roll control and kept wings level. Yaw control was adequate. I made minimal yaw and roll control inputs to avoid a spin and [requested priority handling] with Center; advising loss of control. They asked which airport I requested and I replied I just need to get lower and asked for the freezing level. I observed OAT at 17000 ft. to be approximately 18-20°F and watched it steadily increase as I descended. I found a power setting that would keep the AoA above [the] donut; keeping an adequate IAS while getting 800-1000 FPM descent.At 14000; precipitation was heavy snow and I observed static discharging on the leading edges of the wings via sparks. Around 11000 ft.; I was preparing for the elevators to become unfrozen; as I suspected ice had formed and frozen them in position during the slow climb; and was prepared for a rapid nose down movement. The elevators did break loose and I was able to recover the nose down attitude quickly and accurately with the maneuver similar to a power-on stall recovery. While still descending; I commanded several nose up and nose down control inputs with increasing force to ensure controls were still functioning and ensuring I had not broken anything. I then worked with Center to pick my destination and requested lower to get into rain. I observed light to moderate mixed and clear icing at that time on the wings and increased my IAS. Once I was in the heavy rain; the ice melted and the aircraft remained responsive to all controls with the engine performing nominally. I asked and was given vectors for the RNAV XX approach but was only cleared down to 6000 ft. at ZZZZZ; 3000 ft. higher than the approach depicted. Upon reaching 6000 ft. and turning inbound; I was switched to Advisory and was VMC with the field in sight. I executed a 360 turn to lose altitude and then flew the pattern to further reduce altitude; executing a normal landing in heavy rain on Runway XX. I called Center on the phone to cancel IFR.On the ground; I visually inspected all control surfaces; tested trim and autopilot functions; and removed several panels to inspect the control push-rods; finding no abnormalities. I checked weather; refiled;and continued to my destination at a lower altitude.My desire to stay above the tops at night near the upper limits of adequate climb performance resulted in inadvertent flight into icing conditions. I believe the slow; sustained climb resulted in minimal elevator inputs and adequate time for ice to build up on the counterweights; freezing the elevators in place. I believe I had more clear ice than I could observe via flashlight. I should have avoided the situation by either climbing earlier to ensure [that I] remained clear of the clouds or descended into warmer temperatures. I could have also diverted or turned around. I had already flown 6.5 hours for hire in IFR and hazardous weather conditions in the PC-12 and fatigue was a factor. I was on supplemental oxygen and remained alert and coherent during the entire event. I credit excellent training - power for altitude; pitch for speed - and upset recovery training during PC-12 initial training; to keeping limited control of the aircraft and avoiding a stall; which would have most likely resulted in a stall/spin and fatal crash.

column121: I was acting as a flight instructor on board Aircraft X; a Cessna 172S on a local IFR flight practicing approaches. My student is a Certified Flight Instructor (CFI) candidate who was gaining instrument currency and proficiency. We began with an ILS approach at ZZZ1 with my student flying the aircraft and me handling ATC communications to reduce his workload in the hard IMC conditions. We crossed a cold front while receiving vectors for the ILS approach where we encountered light to moderate turbulence and precipitation. We completed the ILS approach without incident and proceeded to the VOR for the VOR-A approach into ZZZ; planning to complete a Low Approach Only. We experienced severe turbulence which forced the autopilot (GFC700) to disconnect and I took the controls of the aircraft and requested deviations to the north as necessary to track clear of the progressing cold front. Once we got into smoother air; I gave my student the flight controls and we proceeded direct ZZZ2 [VOR] for a procedure turn. Our plan was to complete the VOR-A approach and then receive radar vectors for the RNAV 01 at ZZZ. My student had proclaimed that he wanted to avoid going back through the cold front while getting vectored for the RNAV 01 approach and suggested we circle to land at ZZZ and cancel the IFR flight plan. When my student suggested this; we had passed the Final Approach Fix inbound and began a descent to the Minimum Descent Altitude and were switched over to advisory frequency. I switched frequencies back to Approach to tell them our intentions to try and circle to land since they were expecting us to go missed on the practice approach. When I told ATC of our intentions; they replied in the affirmative and added 'Aircraft X; low altitude alert; check altitude immediately; altitude indicates 1;800.' I replied the altitude checks and requested an altimeter setting. ATC replied with an altimeter setting of 29.58 and we had a setting of 29.67 set in. I figured this was why they gave us the low altitude alert but then quickly realized that the Minimum Descent Altitude for the segment of the approach we were on was 2;020 feet and we were at 1;720 feet with the new altimeter setting. I informed my student to return to 2;020 feet and we continued on the approach without issue and proceeded with the missed approach with vectors to the RNAV01 at ZZZ. During the missed approach; I was surprised at myself that I did not catch that the student had descended below the Minimum Descent Altitude and I assessed why that had happened during a period of smooth flight and during the post flight discussion with my student. During the lead up to the approach; the encounter with the severe turbulence had shaken both me and my student. We also had a back seat passenger who was an instrument student who had never been in IMC before. I was concerned with the safety of my student and the back seat student and began thinking about the circle to land approach and how we would request vectors for the RNAV Approach if we were unable to circle to land in order to stay away from the front line. I had determined from the weather when we departed ZZZ that circling for the runway at ZZZ would have been nearly impossible with the current ceilings. I told my student this and informed him we would need to execute the RNAV Approach in order to make it back into the airport.The workload at the moment was very high and the effects of the turbulence certainly could have impaired multitasking skills for both my student and I. When we began the descent on the approach; we left 3;000 feet for 2;020 feet which is the Minimum Descent Altitude until a fix which then the Minimum Descent Altitude decreases to 1;760 feet. My student did not reset the altitude select when we ran our Final Approach Fix check and the altitude select remained at 3;000 feet. Additionally; when I recognized we were below the published Minimum Descent Altitude; I should have instructed my student to execute the missed approach as 91.175(E)(1)(i) states; rather than just climbing back up to the Minimum Descent Altitude.This flight was also my third flight in hard IMC this day; and this VOR approach was my 8th approach in IMC in a span of 6 hours. I am an experienced Flight Instructor with over 45 hours in actual instrument conditions and over 150 approach logged; but never before had I completed so many IMC flights in such a time span with the challenging conditions of the frontal passage. My self-assessment prior to this flight determined I was able to complete the flight successfully with good quality of instruction to the student; but the extraordinary conditions we experienced during the flight quickly eroded that ability for me; in addition to the highly divided workload situation we found ourselves in while inbound on the VOR Approach which led to the descent below Minimum Descent Altitude and failure to execute the missed approach immediately after. I think also a more comprehensive briefing of the approach would have aided in my student's short term memory of the initial difference of Minimum Descent Altitude. Even though I briefed the Minimum Descent Altitudes; I do not think they were retained due to the stress and workload of the situation. If this event were to occur again; I would better instruct my student to execute the missed approach rather than working to reclaim the missed Minimum Descent Altitude.
column123: The aircraft had 3 people on board for a local approaches flight in IMC conditions in Aircraft. This flight took place while a stationary front was passing through the area. This caused for almost constant moderate turbulence at times during the flight close to the frontal passage. The flight started with an ILS approach into ZZZ1. After the ILS approach we were vectored to go to the ZZZ2 VOR . Along the way; we had to deviate twice for turbulence. This; as well as IMC conditions; was causing a good amount of sensory overload for myself and the flight instructor with me. At times during the flight the autopilot was being used; but at one point; the amount of turbulence actually caused the autopilot to disengage. Because of this; at the time of the deviation; I was hand flying the aircraft while the other pilot was loading the VOR Approach. When we proceeded inbound on the approach; there is a step down to a minimum of 2;020 feet until an 8 DME fix. Then the minimum goes lower to 1;760 feet. With the sensory overload that both I and the other pilot were experiencing during the IMC flight; we ended up descending below the altitude minimum below the fix. ATC had not updated our altimeter setting in a decent amount of time. We were called by ATC letting us know for a low altitude and to immediately recover. They gave us an updated altimeter and our altitude after the correction showed it being right at the approach total minimum. Instead of executing an immediate missed approach we climbed back up to 2020 feet then re-descended to the 1;760 minimums. By doing this we unfortunately broke 14 CFR 91.175 (c) 1; 3 and (e) 1. The proper action would have been to either; not conduct the flight in the first place or; to immediately execute the missed approach once realizing the descent below the step down. We also could have stopped the flight after the ILS approach into ZZZ1. The rest of the flight utilized great CRM; but during this approach; a better action to even ask as the approach started would have been to double check the approach and its minimums including each step down.

He had trouble hearing ATC the entire trip which we attributed to his being off a year. Obviously; there was a breakdown in Verbalize; Verify and Monitor. Lesson learned: especially when tired and in a high-workload environment; strict adherence to SOP is essential.

column121: We checked in at ZZZ for flight to ZZZ1.  Walking onto aircraft to preflight and get ready the FA's (flight attendants) commented that they smelled a strong fume odor in the rear of the cabin.  The prior crew had left the APU running and that was providing the air to the cabin.  We were not immediately sure what it was but the longer we were inside the aircraft the more it seemed to smell all over the aircraft.  One flight attendant soon commented that she had been in a fume smell diversion and that she felt it now smelled exactly like what she had experienced before. As I was contacting Dispatch and Maintenance Control; the ZZZ station without our knowledge or consent had sprayed the entire aft cabin with some kind of disinfectant spray to cover up the smell and had begun to board passengers.  When I was made aware of this I radioed them to stop spraying the aircraft; halt the boarding; and remove the passengers that were onboard.  Maintenance Control had called a contract Maintenance Tech to investigate the odor.  Meanwhile; we had shutdown the APU and connected the ground air. When the Maintenance Tech arrived; he had a bunch of paperwork for items to check; and mentioned that he was going to inspect the APU.  He did not seem to know what to check or how to check it.  Ultimately he handed me the pile of papers and ask us to run the engines.  In an effort to help we did so.  We could not specifically determine the source of the smell; but it seemed stronger with the APU providing air.  We were unable to isolate the source and could not fly the aircraft or do a maintenance ferry flight. Afterward; Maintenance Control then informed us that the residual contamination in the air ducts would have to be cleaned and tested with special equipment; and that they would have to send a road crew down from ZZZ to perform those functions.  So Maintenance Control knew from the start that this type of contamination issue required special procedures and equipment to deal with and withheld that critical information unnecessarily exposing us to who knows what kind of long term health hazards instead of just informing of this up front. After we officially could not use the airplane; it was around XA:30pm.  We were assigned to fly another aircraft for the flight now departing at XG:15pm.  We then spent the next few hours trying to get a day room so we could get a meal and away from the airport before the later flight.  Each time were verbally told we had a room from Crew Tracking; Hotel Desk; etc.; we called the hotel and were told there were no such rooms available for us.  After wasting a considerable amount of time on this effort we were finally given rooms and arrived at the hotel just after XF:00pm. I walked down the highway from the hotel to find something to eat after having nothing for several hours.  Finally sitting down to eat a sandwich; I realized that I had a dull headache from trying to determine if the fumes were no longer present in the aircraft when isolating certain ducts for Maintenance Control.  It dawned on me that I was fatigued and I reported this to Crew Tracking. The cause was Maintenance; fume smells; lack of timely day room. [Captain suggested] better communications with Maintenance and Dispatch.

column121: I reviewed the maintenance log when I arrived at the aircraft for the first flight of the day. It had just been released from maintenance. It had previously been written up for a strong smell coming from the lavatory. The corrective action stated that the lavatory had been leaking into the cargo bay. It had been repaired the same day and I was the first to fly the aircraft. I included this information with my crew brief.During the descent to ZZZ1; sometime prior to FL180 because the descent checklist had yet to be completed; the FO (First Officer) and I heard what sounded like an extra loud flushing noise from the FWD LAV (Forward Lavatory); but then developed into a loud sound similar to an engine spooling down; immediately followed by a strange; slightly chemical odor. We both looked at each other and confirmed what we heard and smelled. I called the A F/A (Flight Attendant) to verify if anyone had just flushed the toilet. She said someone was in the lavatory; had just flushed; and it smelled strongly like excrement.The odor quickly subsided. We discussed the possible sources. The LAV was a different style from most of our aircraft so it could have just been a sound [different] than what we were used to. The LAV had just been repaired so the odor could have been related. Since there odor was gone and there were no other indications of abnormality we continued to ZZZ1 but I had the FO start reviewing synoptic pages for any clues and I started reviewing possible diversion airports. We made a list of airports closest to our position as we got closer to ZZZ1; ZZZ2; then ZZZ3; then ZZZ4.During descent after passing through FL180; I started to hear and feel the aircraft surging. It sounded like it was coming from the engines. I de-cluttered the EICAS to check for vibration. There was a notable difference in engine vibration; but they were still in the green and there were no other indications on the EICAS.At approximately 13;000 ft. the FO and I both noticed a strong acrid odor. I called the A F/A who confirmed the LAV was not in use. I then called for the Smoke; Fire; Fumes QRC (Quick Reference Checklist). We donned our oxygen masks and the FO started through the QRC. We were almost exactly on top of ZZZ3; which we had already decided as a suitable airport; so when the FO [read the steps related to ATC] of the QRH (Quick Reference Handbook) I told him to [request priority handling] and ask to land at ZZZ3 immediately.ATC assigned an ALT of 9;000 ft. As I started to descend; the aircraft began shaking violently. ATC continued to vector and assign lower altitudes. When the FO turned off the RECIRC fans per the QRH; I asked him to put the checklist down and set up the aircraft for landing. We were very close to the airport and descending quickly. I decided the priority was for the FO to get our landing numbers and set up the approach while coordinating with ATC and the FA's. I could not help because I suspected external damage to the control surfaces so I did not want to take my attention away from maintaining positive control of the aircraft.Somewhere around the 9;000 ft. mark or lower we received an EICAS PACK 1 FAIL. This was the first time the EICAS provided any kind of indication of an abnormality. We had experienced a loud noise; strong odors; violent shaking; and now a PACK 1 FAIL. It felt as if the aircraft had suffered major damage and safe completion of the flight was at serious risk. ATC had placed us on a downwind for the ILS but; fearing we may be losing more systems and controllability; I told the FO we were turning immediately to final. As we slowed to approach speeds the shaking reduced. The FO contacted the FA's to go over [procedures]. I did not order a brace and I did not intend to evacuate. The aircraft was stabilizing and there weren't any smoke or fire indications in the cabin or flight deck. I landed and stopped on the runway. I requested an inspection by the fire trucks to make sure the aircraft wasn't on fire and we were safe to taxi. I made an announcement for everyone to remain seated and that we had landed due to a maintenance issue; but that the aircraft was safe and we were taxiing to a gate.In our judgement; due to the order and severity of events; we thought the aircraft may be in serious jeopardy. An immediate landing was the safest option available. I have often conducted a very similar scenario with FO's on long flights out of the area and near ZZZ3; during cruise. The scenario is a fume event. The reason this is important is because the QRH for fumes is very long and involves a lot of system isolation for troubleshooting. It would take 20-30 minutes for us to review the QRH in a relaxed; stable environment. Only at the end of the QRH do you see just how much runway would be required if you're heavy and have taken a lot of performance penalties due to the QRH troubleshooting process. Because we were so close to the airport and descending quickly; I prioritized performance and navigation over completing the QRH. There simply was not enough time for the full checklist.Parked at the gate; I called Dispatch and explained what was going on. They weren't aware of the diversion. The FO had asked ATC to notify our company during descent. I was getting bounced around a lot between Dispatch and [Administration] with Maintenance talking to them in the background; but Maintenance immediately insisted that it was a simple air system failure and that the aircraft was safe. Both the FO and I conducted a walk-around. I said the aircraft was not safe to fly. I wouldn't have landed in ZZZ3 if I thought the aircraft was safe. This aircraft needs a full maintenance inspection based on the severity of conditions we had just experienced. [In the past] I've had a hydraulic line rupture at FL200; I've had a brake failure on landing; I've had a full system failure. This was like nothing I had experienced and felt far more severe at the time than just a simple air system failure. It was serious enough that I didn't know if we would make the runway. This aircraft had a recent history of fluids leaking into the cargo bay. How much unseen damage was caused by these fluids? Why wouldn't an inspection be required if the maintenance department is saying 'oh yeah the smell and shaking is from the system blowing out'? As I'm trying to convince Dispatch and Maintenance that an inspection needs to be conducted; this is already approaching about 2 hours after landing; the adrenaline started to fade and the fatigue settled in. The entire crew was exhausted to the point that even the FA's were fatigued. Having drilled this scenario; I believe I acted appropriately given the circumstances. QRH calls for system isolation to identify the source but with odor being cause of the [diversion] and no EICAS indications there is no way to verify the source without taking the O2 mask off; which is extremely dangerous. We were so close and working with so little time that getting on the ground immediately became the top priority.

column121: Upon finishing my three-day paring in ZZZ1 at (time/date) I received a phone call from Scheduling; as I was leaving the aircraft. They told me they had added on to my schedule; they needed me to deadhead to ZZZ; then ferry an aircraft back to ZZZ1. I was concerned because I had already flown quite a bit that day and was afraid that I would not be legal for it. The Scheduler assured me that I was legal and that it was all okay. I asked them to look into it again because I had my doubts. I then asked if they could provide a hotel for rest at the end of the turn as I would be extremely tired. She claimed she would pass it on to the hotel desk. Upon contacting the hotel desk they said they could only provide a room if there was an unused ZZZ1 overnight room; which there was not.I proceeded onto the gate for the first leg of the ZZZ turn. Inside 30 minutes to departure there was no crew or other deadheading crewmember present at the aircraft. The flight to ZZZ was scheduled completely empty except for the Operating Crew; myself and one other deadheader. Again; I was concerned that I would time out before we could complete the turn so took it upon myself to prepare the aircraft for departure and set up the cockpit for the Operating Crew; in order to expedite our departure. We eventually departed 18 minutes later than planned. Upon reaching ZZZ; the operating First Officer left to recover a diverted aircraft back to ZZZ1 and I quickly prepared our aircraft for our return to ZZZ1. Unfortunately; once again; our aircraft experienced multiple delays due to random unexplainable maintenance locks; issues with load and balance calculation and performance. As we sat on the ramp at ZZZ I could tell that I would soon be in danger of timing out and verified my legalities. It showed a Table B Limit of XX42C without extension. At roughly XXX25CI called Crew Scheduling and notified them I was within 20 minutes of reaching the latest takeoff limit; and asked them what their plan was. The Scheduler on the line said that there was someone looking into my legalities and that they would call me back. That call never came. Shortly thereafter the aircraft issues were resolved and we were able to depart at XX37CF; just five minutes before the XX42C takeoff limit. With the aid of computer program and the printed crew legalities sheet; it appeared we had taken off within limits and were completely legal to fly the flight.Upon landing at ZZZ1 at XX04C; we were told that there were no gates available we would have to hold on the pad until one became available. Shortly after parking in the pad; we received an ACARS message referencing my employee number and requesting a flight delay extension. It showed several times; but those times did not match any times on the calculator on computer program. It was confusing and seemed to be in error. Since we were parked in the pad with the parking brake set; the Captain took the radios and I called Crew Scheduling. I explained we were on the ground waiting for a gate; I told them I had received the ACARS message and that it did not make sense - I asked for clarification and the implications of accepting or rejecting. They placed me on a brief hold but when they came back they were not able to answer any of my questions and essentially didn't seem too concerned since we were on the ground in ZZZ1. Since Crew Scheduling was not able to explain the ACARS message I neither accepted nor rejected the extension. Once again I asked for a hotel room; and they said they were not able to accommodate.A gate finally opened; we terminated the aircraft and I left the gate. As I was walking away I got a call from Crew Scheduling; a different Scheduler was on the line telling me that I had violated the limits. I explained to him that I had taken off five minutes before the limit time and that I should have been legal to fly the flight. The Scheduler explained that even though that was true I had violated the 'Last Block In' time of XX15C. I told him that I was not aware of any Last Block In Time; it is not a number that is published or provided to us in the cockpit; either by the Crew legalities sheet or the computer calculator. I also explained that I had called Crew Scheduling multiple times this evening to voice my concern over my proximity to the limits and not once during any of those calls did any member of Crew Scheduling even bother to mention a 'Last Block In' time limitation. The Scheduler tried to explain that it was all okay as long I say I was aware of it and that I was in acceptance. I countered that no; I was not aware of the limit despite my multiple requests to Crew Scheduling to evaluate my limits; and no; I was not aware I had exceeded any limit; yet when I called for an explanation of the ACARS message; it would have been the perfect time to tell me; and finally no; I did not accept the extension; nor did I reject it because nobody at Crew Scheduling could explain it to me. However; by default; a lack of acceptance should be considered a rejection. This was obviously not what the Scheduler wanted to hear; so he told me that he would forward it to a Supervisor; who would subsequently call my Chief Pilot. I said that was fine; asked that he have the Supervisor call me as well and we ended the call.This experience has taught me that Company does not have either the capability or the desire to adequately protect its pilots from exceeding FAR Part 117 Flight Duty Limitations and Rest Requirement restrictions. I understand that FAR 117 responsibilities are shared between the certificate holder (Company) and the pilot (myself). In this case; however; the pilot had expressed concern about the limits three times; asked for clarification from the certificate holder; yet was repeatedly stonewalled with evasive or non-existent guidance in order to complete the operation. Finally; after successfully and safely completing that operation the pilot was criticized for exceeding a limit the he was never provided; warned of; or explained ahead of time. Then finally the certificate holder attempted to coerce the pilot into accepting the extension after the fact.Resolution of this issue and prevention in the future should include: 1. Provide pilots with the latest block-in time on the crew legalities sheet and computer in additions to latest takeoff times for every flight. This allows pilots to clearly understand all limits of the flight. 2. Better and/or more extensive training of Crew Schedulers on FAR Part 117 duty restrictions. 3. Clearer and more proactive communication from Crew Scheduling to pilots about approaching limits. 4. Make available crew rest accommodations; on request; to a pilot that has been flown to the extent of or over the flight limits on the last day of a paring. Accident prevention should extend beyond the confines of the cockpit. After working 13 hours and 48 minutes on duty operating aircraft; nobody should be behind the wheel of a motor vehicle late at night.
column123: This event involves a potential exceedance of the Part 117 Maximum Block In (MBI) time for the First Officer at the end of a long duty day that included a re-route (involuntary assignment). It has already been reported by the First Officer; and I agree with and support his report. Rather than repeat his whole narrative; I will highlight important points and add one or two additional observations.In ZZZ; we experienced multiple unexplained maintenance locks which prevented us from receiving takeoff data. (Unknown if this malfunction was due to the new maintenance software; or ZZZ Ops not entering our actual fuel on board - which was tankered in and approximately 3;000 pounds more than expected on the release.) After about 30 minutes; we were able to resolve the situation by correcting fuel on board on a new release (and new takeoff reference number.) Feeling pressure to simultaneously deal with First Officer's legality issue while resolving the maintenance lock issue was a distraction and threat that (unlike weather; passenger issues; or aircraft malfunctions) is created by the system. In other words; although Part 117 is intended to help improve safety; the way it's applied ends up being an unhelpful distraction and a threat to safety.The First Officer tried to raise legality questions on the original call. Later; during the re-assignment; the First Officer called Scheduling at least three times to try to discuss the situation. Although I could not hear the other end of the conversations; it sounded like each time he was told they were aware of it and 'working on it.'The First Officer had accepted an extension the previous night. This caused him / us to wonder whether he was even legal for an extension on a 2nd consecutive night? He attempted to bring this up to Scheduling but never got a good answer from them. (Like everything else in Part 117; it's not as easy to answer as it should be. It certainly isn't a yes/no answer.)Once on the ground in ZZZ1 and holding in the pad for a gate to become available; we received an automated ACARS message asking to accept or reject an extension. This was done at the very last minute; when the only realistic options were: accept the extension; or violate Part 117. That doesn't really give the pilot any option to reject the extension. As previously stated; he had already been trying to work with Scheduling prior to this. And; he also (unsuccessfully) attempted to clarify his block in time and options with Scheduling after the ACARS message. When there was still time to address the issue; Scheduling would only give him a 'we're working on it.' It seems like the only option Scheduling would consider was strong-arming him into accepting the extension 'or else.' As we approach what looks to be a very busy summer flying schedule; with the strong possibility that the pilots being brought back in July from extended time off will arrive on the line too late to fill the gaps; Scheduling and Dispatch might consider being more proactive looking for other solutions (offering more premium open time trips; not diverting aircraft into airports where we only have one scheduled flight per day; etc.) versus pushing so hard and flirting with legality issues. In the interest of fatigue management and safety; I don't think it's reasonable to assume that a pilot who has been involuntarily reassigned more flying at the end of a long trip will automatically desire to voluntarily accept an extension to his flight duty limits. The discussion needs to happen much earlier; and not through an automated message giving the false appearance the pilot has an actual choice in the matter.

column121: Last night I flew the airplane across the border from ZZZZ to ZZZ to clear Customs on my way to ZZZ1. Customs held me for about 30 minutes. I was quite tired and stressed because this flight was scheduled very suddenly and I had to drive to ZZZZ to make the flight. By the time I was released from Customs; jumped in the airplane; started the engines; and tried to get my clearance to ZZZ1; ZZZ Tower was long closed. So I tried a phone call to TRACON first; but since ZZZ is so close to the border; my cell phone could not get the proper signal; between Mexico and U.S.; so the call did not go through. At that moment; I switched the ZZZ Tower frequency to see if I could get my clearance from TRACON with no success. So; I decided to taxi to the head of Runway XXR; and try it again there. No joy. I began to feel desperate. I tried again calling by phone and this time I made contact; but the call dropped in a second. I kept trying for about four times; until I finally could get my clearance.My 'void if not off by' time was about 8 minutes; so I rushed the flight plan into the FMS; and put Tower frequency again in Comm 1. I then made the call that I was taking off from ZZZ for a straight out departure. Nobody answered; so I began my take off run. I saw some lights down the runway but; from my perspective; looked beyond the runway. Only when I was about to rotate realized and almost froze to see what I think was a helicopter on the runway! I pulled hard on the yoke; since I could not stop the airplane on the ground without hitting the other aircraft. I tried to calm myself down as I was scared to death. I was surprised that I did not hear the helicopter on the Tower frequency. That is when I realized I had not put in the correct Tower frequency! My blood went to my feet and my heart was racing and I felt so bad and miserable to think I could have killed some innocent people along with myself just for that 'little' error. I still feel awful.From now on; I will double and triple check my frequencies; altitudes; headings and runway holding instructions. I assure you that I learned my lesson on how external factors as stress and fatigue can and will affect your judgment. I will do my best to prevent this from happening to me again. Just the thought of the terrible disaster I might have caused; makes me realize the importance of proper focus; concentration and compliance with SOP's; no matter how tired you are. Besides; I will try to fly with a copilot from now on. Another set of eyes and mind are better than one.

column121: We were given an ILS clearance into ZZZ in VMC conditions. A VFR airplane was at our altitude and seemed to be tracking to cross the final approach course. We both had the aircraft in sight and changed to a visual approach to maneuver behind the aircraft. At that point the airplane made a sharp right turn and we had to turn further right (away from the final approach course) to maintain separation. It seemed like the plane was on a long final for ZZZ1 and we were then at 90 degrees off of the final approach and unable to make a stable approach into ZZZ. We called the go-around with Tower and were given a heading and altitude toward the east before switching to Approach Control to come back and try it again.The main issue was the VFR traffic no one was communicating with. The crew did not fully brief the location and potential for conflicting traffic for ZZZ1 when approaching from the south. Had the crew not changed to a visual approach and been given ATC vectors; we may not have had the same issues. A go-around may not have been avoidable due to conflicting traffic but a more thorough brief of the airspace and threats may have increased situational awareness and avoided confusion. We should also have not changed the type of approach at the last minute.
column123: We were given a heading to intercept the localizer to Runway XXL and given a traffic call that was not on frequency. Controller then had us maintain heading and fly through the localizer to avoid traffic which was about 500 ft. above; crossing our path and that of the localizer track. We decided as a crew that if they gave us clearance for the visual; we could maintain separation from the aircraft into ZZZ. We were given just that and made the right turn back towards the runway and began to descend for landing. The general aviation aircraft ahead of us descended into our path and made an unexpected turn as we were continuing. I disconnected the autopilot and continued the turn towards the east to avoid ZZZ3 airspace and aircraft. Once clear of the aircraft; we elected to scrap the approach and were given vectors for another uneventful approach. We were originally on a 5 mile final to Runway XYR when ZZZ swapped runway configuration and we were then rerouted to the south to land north. We briefed the new approach and had the approach loaded and armed. With the change of runways; perhaps there was not enough time to fully brief the new approach and surroundings to point out a runway to the east that could cause some confusion. Some cumulative fatigue was present; as well as it being our third of four legs for the day added to the stress of the situation. I do think the spacing given into ZZZ was a partial factor with a GA aircraft that wasn't talking to anyone. There are steps to help mitigate issues like this; like ensuring complete situational awareness of self and the possibility of others; but ultimately there might always be general aviation aircraft out there operating around controlled airspace's not on frequency.

column121: On arrival at ZZZ; winds were variable and began to favor Runway XX for landing. We were set up for landing on Runway XY. I; acting as Pilot Monitoring for this leg due to special qualification airport; suggested to Captain that we swap our planned arrival runway due to winds and additional available landing distance (approximately 500 feet) for landing on Runway XX. The FMC was reprogrammed correctly; briefed; and we accepted a heading to intercept final Runway XX. With approximately a 30 degree intercept; approach control cleared us for the ILS XX. Captain selected approach mode early. This caused the aircraft to capture a false glideslope and the aircraft began a descent prior to capturing the localizer. I called this to the Captain's attention; of which he was also aware.Prior to localizer capture I recommended a discontinued approach. Altitude was well above Minimum Safe Altitude and the approach was salvageable but due to my experience level in the jet; I suggested a soft go-around. The Captain elected to continue; to which I agreed and remarked that our subsequent protected altitude would be 2;600 feet; which we were currently above; and that I would monitor. The Captain; slightly flustered about the false glideslope capture began to fiddle with Auto Pilot disconnect; Flight Director reset; and approach mode was re-armed. The new capture mode now is LOC but with a failed Glideslope. The aircraft has defaulted into the current vertical speed. I call slightly below glideslope; Captain again resets Auto pilot; Flight Director; and re-arms the approach mode. Localizer captures; Glideslope has been armed; and we are currently in a 700 to 800 FPM descent; very slightly low on Glideslope; at a safe speed; and safe altitude.I call attention to our protected Final Approach Fix altitude and glideslope intercept at ZZZZZ 2238 feet. If I remember correctly; we were approximately 3 miles from ZZZZZ when I remarked that at our current Flight Path Angle would have us slightly below our target altitude without any correction at ZZZZZ. Let me be clear; the aircraft was; based on our current descent rate; projected to be only slightly below 2;300 feet at the Final Approach Fix. A minor correction would have rectified the approach path angle and captured the glideslope. I called our altitude to the Captains attention once more approximately 1 to 2 miles prior to ZZZZZ; where we had now reached 2;300 feet; the charted approach value. Right as I was going to call for the Go Around at ZZZZZ; the tower controller issued a Low Altitude Alert; the Go Around was called and initiated; and the aircraft was at approximately 2;100 feet; a little less than 200 feet low at the charted glideslope intercept altitude; as well as above 1;000 feet above ground.The Go-Around was accomplished without error and a subsequent ILS was flown to Runway XX without any additional complications. Upon debrief; I became aware that the Captain was unaware that he had not captured the Glideslope. I re-framed the situation for us to consider alternate action and explained my reasoning for a requested discontinued approach prior to localizer capture. I am still low time and in consolidation. I had no reason to expect that we could not become stable with glideslope capture prior to Final Approach Fix. Hindsight is exactly that and this event began and ended all within 4 miles. The Go-round was completed to qual standards with safety and stable approach criteria in mind.False glideslopes capture prior to localizer capture due to not allowing the aircraft to capture in LOC or LNAV prior to arming the approach mode. Again; I believe I was very clear about our impending altitude deviation; however I don't believe I heard any response from the Captain from 3 miles(my initial call) and 1 to 2 miles(my second que). I could be wrong. The whole event spanned a time frame of less than 3 minutes from 'looks good' to 'doesn't look so good' so I could NOT have fit many more altitude callouts in that span. Due to my low experience in the jet; I incorrectly expected a correction that I did not receive. The go around was initiated at or just seconds after the Final Approach Fix. An assumption of understanding is not the greatest way to handle approaching a go around. I do not believe I was hinting and hoping but I will be more aggressive with my descent planning awareness callouts so as not to enter into a [undesirable situation] in the future. However; the correct decision was made concerning the safe operation of the aircraft and the proper response was executed.
column123: Trip was third leg of the day.  Landed from second leg at around XA:40 local and got to sleep room at XB:10L.  Awakened 30 early of show time at approximately XB:40L.  Weather was marginal regionally and at ZZZ. ZZZ1 was filed alternate but also monitored weather at ZZZ2 for second option.  First Officer has less than 75 hours and ZZZ is Special Qual field. Identified the CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain) hazard; short runway; marginal weather; etc.  Pre briefed the ILS XY enroute as winds were favoring that runway.  Also talked about EFVS (Enhanced Flight Vision Systems) and auto land contingencies.  Upon contacting ZZZ approach; they asked if we wanted ILS XX due to a wind shift.  Initially decided to stick with XY but reversed the decision seconds later due to shorter usable runway on XY due to displaced threshold and winds favoring XX slightly.I was flying the approach while the First Officer set up and briefed the ILS XX.  We re-accomplished the approach checklist and accepted a clearance direct to the Final Approach Fix to cross at 2;600 feet and maintain until established; cleared for the ILS.  We put the 2;600 foot hard restriction at the Final Approach Fix and were navigating LNAV/VNAV.  Just prior to Final Approach Fix I mistakenly selected the approach mode.  The aircraft immediately intercepted what I believe was a false glide slope and begun to descend before intended.  I turned off both flight directors and attempted to get the aircraft out of approach mode. The aircraft stayed in approach mode because I did not disengage the autopilot.  So; after re-engaging the aircraft tracked the localizer in LOC mode and Vertical Speed with Glideslope Flight Mode Annunciation struck through as a failed mode.  Realizing the error; I disconnected both flight directors and autopilot and immediately re-engaged and re-automated.  At this point I believe the aircraft momentarily intercepted a glide path; and almost immediately and simultaneously with the Tower Controller realized we were about 250 feet low of the glide slope intercept altitude.  We immediately performed a discontinued approach and climbed to 3;000 feet.  We received vectors for another ILS XX and auto landed uneventfully.Fatigue was undeniably a root cause although not the only issue here.  Flying two legs and then getting only 30 minutes opportunity to nap between legs was just a little too much for me despite 'feeling pretty good' ahead of the flight involved. In retrospect I should have used LNAV/VNAV to get solidly on the ILS final before selecting approach mode.  And; also; I should have and will in the future decide to discontinue an approach as soon as any serious mode switching starts happening on the final approach. In the light of day and after a nap I know this solidly; but it is much more difficult with a foggy brain at XF:00.  So; in the future; I'm going to use LNAV/VNAV more and not use APP until later in the approach. Revision of the flight pairing to allow for more rest time...even an hour nap; would help.  Also; making sure to use LNAV/VNAV and protect GSIA (Glide Slope Intercept Altitude) at 1 NM prior to the intermediate fix.

column121: During the pre-start check; the crew confirmed that all three altimeters were set properly.  I have a clear memory of personally checking all 3 altimeters.  As Pilot Flying I was hand flying a vectored departure and given a clearance to climb and maintain 10;000 ft.  Approximately 200 ft prior; as I was leveling off; I was given a new clearance to climb and maintain 16;000 ft.  I continued to hand fly and completed a smooth level off at 16;000.  As I was doing so; ATC gave us a notification of opposite direction traffic 1;000 feet above us which we had on TCAS and immediately saw visually.  All appeared normal and I believed ATC was simply letting us know why we had not been cleared higher and was giving a normal notification of traffic.  The transmission was partially garbled; and the Pilot Monitoring (PM) requested that ATC repeat it.  ATC simply responded with 'maintain 16;000' which the PM acknowledged.  The PM then noticed that our altimeters did not agree and informed me that my altimeter was set at 29.92 instead of the local altimeter setting.  I reset the altimeter and discovered that I was actually at 16;180 ft; which likely had prompted the call from ATC.  We were just short of 200 ft high.  I descended and was at 16;000 before passing under the opposite direction traffic.  We did not receive a TCAS TA or RA.  I have no memory of resetting my altimeter to 29.92 but surmise that I must have done so as it would be very difficult to have hit the button accidentally.  While allowed to set 29.92 once assigned a climb above 18;000 ft; my normal practice is to wait until the altimeter setting flashes approaching 18;000 ft to reset it.  Normal practice meaning I don't recall ever doing it differently.  I cannot explain when I reset it to standard; except that it was after the pre-start check and prior to leveling at 16;000.  My best guess is that I did so at 10;000 for some reason; as that was the only altitude I passed that I would have considered significant; although I was on profile in a 250 knot climb both before and after 10;000 ft.  In this case; the local altimeter setting was close enough to standard that I did not exceed the 300 feet limit for a flight violation or cause a traffic conflict.  This was just luck however.  Had the altimeter been significantly different from standard; I don't believe I would have been more likely to notice the error and could have been responsible for a conflict.I'm not sure what the cause was except that I simply made an error.  Why; how; or when escapes me.  However; I did have to call in fatigued that morning as we were on a late in the day pairing but had been delayed overnight to a morning departure two time zones to the east.  When I called in fatigued unable to fall asleep early; I was given my 10 hours and a later show time; though to make the later show time I still needed to get out of bed two hours prior to when I was accustomed.  After I woke up to my alarm; I was notified that the aircraft was still in maintenance and was given an even later show time; and I took a short nap.  In the end; the error happened during a time I'd normally be awake; but I did not get my normal sleep routine.  I had legal rest and did not feel particularly fatigued; but I can't discount that fatigue very well could have contributed to such an unusual error.  I utilized the Fatigue Risk Management Plan (FRMP) to the extent I felt necessary and neither Crew Scheduling nor the company pressured me in any way to fly fatigued.  Perhaps I should have insisted on an even later show time.  My feeling of responsibility to our customers who had already been delayed over 12 hours was a factor in making a show time that was earlier than normal for me; considering time zones; but again; I didn't feel overly tired at the time. Obviously; having made this error for the first time; I'll be more cognizant of when I hit the button to bring the altimeter to standard going forward.  As far as the possible fatigueaspect; our promise to our customers to transport them to their destination at the time we say can sometimes conflicts with our promise to transport them as safely as possible.  I have availed myself of the risk management plan several times in the last year and have never received any negative feedback or pressure to fly fatigued.  There are times when I feel the probability of losing pay has pressured other pilots to fly with less rest than they needed; but in this case pay was not a factor as I was the only pilot available to fly this leg to an outstation serviced only once per day.  So; I was going to be paid for the leg no matter when I flew it.  Therefore; I can't recommend any changes to the risk management plan.  I simply need to do a better job of anticipating and assessing my own fatigue level.
column123: Climbing out we were assigned to maintain 16;000 ft. First Officer (FO) was pilot flying. Altitude was verified at '1;000 to go' call. As we went through 15;000 feet; I said 15;000 climbing 16;000. FO was hand flying; as we near 16;000 (about 100ft to go) I noticed he wasn't slowing down the climb rate. I looked over and his altimeter was set to 29.92 instead of the altimeter we've gotten when I checked in of 30.16. As I looked over ATC asked if we had the 16;000 ft altitude assigned which I replied affirmatively. As I was done talking to ATC I told the FO he had the wrong altimeter setting; and that our Altimeter was 30.16. FO did level off at 16;000 ft but he had a wrong altimeter setting. FO may have pushed the standard 29.92 altimeter inadvertently at some point after initial departure. As the altimeter were set and cross checked for departure on the ground. We had checked our level off altitude on the 1;000 to go call. But I didn't notice at that time he had a wrong altimeter setting. I think on the 1;000 feet to go call we should have notice this discrepancy; but I was looking at my PFD and not his. FO should have mentioned that his altitude did not match with mine at the 1;000 to go call.

column123: Initially set up and briefed for the ILS XX. New ATIS was obtained with runway change to XYR just prior to runway transition point on the ZZZZZ Arrival.  Re briefed and set up for ILS XYR. column121: As this report is not timely; it is to the best of my recollection. Approach phase of the flight to DEN. Briefed and installed the SSKII 2 RNAV/ILS 16R. On arrival we a received multiple speed and heading changes but we were back on course and LNAV/VNAV path were engaged. At some point prior to CLIFF; for whatever reason ATC changed clearance to RNAV 16R for us and the Aircraft (AC) behind us. I was Pilot Not Flying (PNF) so I installed the approach/transition. The AC ahead of us was in sight and was on the arrival but still assigned the ILS 16R. The approach was verified by both the First Officer (FO) and myself. LNAV/VNAV were still engaged and the speed window was open as ATC had already been assigning speed changes. The FO located the Approach briefing guide for the RNAV/RNP approach and RNP values for the approach were line selected and installed. All altitudes for the approach were verified.  I made the comment that 'Since ATC has been messing with our speed so much; the speed window is already open'. So far the approach was flawless and the aircraft (AC) was on the vertical and lateral profile.Upon reaching CLIFF the AC began a descent as it should have. TDZ had been set and VNAV Path was engaged. As we approached CEPEE the MCP/FMA's had not changed SPD/LNAV/VNAV path were engaged. The magenta track depicted CLIFF;CEPEE;AAGEE;JABRO;JETSN; RW 16R; as it should. It was upon arrival at CEPEE that the event occurred. The AC continued to descend and VNAV path remained engaged. But; the AC continued to track straight ahead. CEPEE had not become active and the vector leg out of CLIFF was still engaged. I had been so concerned with the vertical profile that I failed to notice CEPEE was not active. Realizing what had happened I went to the FMC to LS AAGEE; but ATC noticed at the same time and assigned us either a 080 or 090 heading. ATC also canceled the RNAV approach clearance for the AC behind us. We landed without further issue. Once inside the terminal; still pissed that I allowed this to happen; I located the Captain of the AC that landed behind us to apologize. He informed us that ATC had mistakenly given him the # to call. I took the number (#) and called immediately. After a conversation with the supervisor I was informed that there was no safety issue; no loss of separation; and no need to file a report.Looking back; how this could have been avoided... first of all; I could have just said 'unable' when ATC switched us to the RNAV RNP 16R. Although not a big deal at the time...after flying all night; briefing and installing one arrival and approach then; at the last minute being reassigned to a RNAV/ RNP approach which requires lots of briefing and changes; and programming; was probably not the thing to do. What else could I have done...I allowed myself to get distracted. I should have continually monitored the lateral path to insure the AC was doing what we thought it was going to do. It was very clear and it was easy to look outside to follow traffic. It was also the FO's first Pilot Flying leg so there was instruction taking place and attention was diverting to multiple places.The FO did a great job when we were reassigned to the RNAV RNP Z 16R. He did not miss a checklist; procedure; or setting.I'm disgusted that I allowed this to happen. I am unfortunately or fortunately very familiar with the airspace and lateral/ vertical deviation issues in the area. I'm not the first and sure won't be the last; but I know what I will and won't do next time.
column123: During the SSKII 2 RNAV Arrival phase; we were advised by ATC to expect the ILS 16R approach. A few minutes prior to CLFFF; the last point on the SSKII 2 arrival; we were assigned the RNAV (RNP) Z R16R approach. We were on a northerly heading in HDG mode at this time for vectors for the previously expected ILS. The Captain; as Pilot Monitoring (PM); selected the correct RNAV Z 16R approach as well as the correct transition (CLFFF transition) in the FMC. I verified the selected approach and transition after he did so. I then set up the approach per all steps of the Approach Briefing Guide and briefed the approach. We were then given direct CLFFF and selected LNAV. We were cleared for the RNAV RNP Z R16R approach shortly before arriving at CLFFF. Upon arriving at CLFFF; I verified that the CLFFF waypoint sequenced in the FMC to ensure we were now on a published segment of the approach. I selected LNAV; VNAV; opened the speed window for the appropriate speed; requested the PM set touchdown zone elevation (which he did); and verified that the ENGAGED FMA's were in green LNAV and VPATH. The aircraft began a descent per the VPATH glide slope. I ran through the items again to verify that the approach was proceeding correctly. I verified again that the FMA's showed an engaged green LNAV and engaged green VPATH. The approach was proceeding as expected. At the CEPEE waypoint; the aircraft should have begun a right turn towards the AAGEE as part of the track towards the final approach point and final approach course. The aircraft did not turn and continued in a straight course after passing CEPEE. I immediately checked the FMA's again to ensure it did not revert to HDG mode. The FMA's were still in green; engaged LNAV and VPATH. The aircraft was also still in an expected VPATH descent to the TDZE. Within a few seconds; and before we could figure out why the aircraft did not turn; ATC called to cancel the RNAV approach and gave us a right turn for a visual approach to runway 16R and gave clearance for the visual approach. We proceeded uneventfully for the visual approach and landing. After arriving at the gate and leaving the aircraft; a pilot from another aircraft that was behind us during the arrival and approach advised us that he was mistakenly given a phone number by ATC to call regarding the RNAV Z 16R turning issue that we actually experienced. We got the phone number from him and the Captain called. The ATC supervisor said that no report would be required; there was no loss of separation; there was no safety issue; and how just wanted to know what happened. The Captain and I reviewed everything we did in setting up; preparing; and executing that approach and could not figure any reason why the aircraft did not initiate a turn at CEPEE and continued straight while engaged in LNAV with the proper approach waypoints; altitudes; and sequencing verified in the FMC.

column121: Shortly after touchdown on Runway XX the plane began drifting to the left; controllability was deteriorating rapidly. The SIC was attempting to correct the drifting; I (the PIC/PM) stated we're drifting left and applied Full; Authoritative; Firm pressure to the right rudder.  The plane began to straighten out and correct right. The left tires were on the edge of the runway next to the grass and water runoff; causing hydroplaning. As the plane decelerated I was able to regain control and corrected back to the center of the runway. The SIC further assisted in maintaining control of the aircraft as we could feel the tires slipping and hydroplaning. With team work and crew coordination; we regained full control of the Aircraft again and we're able to stop and clear the runway onto a taxiway.Contributing factors include; but not limited to: Weather; rain; winds/crosswinds; darkness/night; unfamiliar airport; wet runway; uncontrolled airport; fresh grass clippings and water pooling along edge of runway; long duty day greater than 12 hours;  consecutive long duty days; multiple flights in a duty day (4th);  human factors; pilot/crew exhaustion; crew dehydration due to extreme heat and humidity throughout the day; high stress loads throughout the day; get there itis; external pressure from passengers;  crews desire to succeed and make everyone happy by completing the mission.
column123: After touchdown the aircraft began to drift to the left. Control correction was applied as the aircraft was drifting but with very little effect. As we neared the left edge of the runway the Pilot Monitoring (PM) assisted the Pilot Flying (PF) and applied full right rudder.  Due to the water collecting on the runway the aircraft did not respond very well to the rudder input until we decelerated.  At that point we had drifted slightly off the runway edge onto the grass. With crew coordination we were able to recover the aircraft back to the runway center line. We excited the runway without further incident.Contributing factors:Weather; fatigue; hot temperatures and humidity throughout the day; dehydration; lack of nutrition; end of a long duty day (arrived at ZZZ on hour 13) preceded by multiple long duty days.This event has opened my eyes a little wider to the complexity of risk assessment. In the future more emphasis will be placed on assessing external pressure; fatigue; and physiological needs.  Also more assertiveness towards these areas of risk assessment. ADM is a very complex system of checks and balances and awareness to even the slightest deviation can prevent future contributing factors to this and other events. A lot could be benefited from a personal assessment matrix to pair with a flight risk assessment matrix to help with mitigating a go/no go decision.

column123: When climbing through 31;000 feet; both the FO and I noticed a distinct odor that smelled like burning toast. We immediately asked the FA if she smelled it as well and she did. column121: While on our first attempt to land at COD we were vectored onto the RNAV to Runway 4 visual conditions prevailed and we were using the RNAV primarily for additional terrain clearance continuous moderate turbulence and windshear persisted on the arrival. ATC vectors and my attempts to maintain an airspeed that buffered against the rapid ups and downs of the green line and the rapid fluctuations of the indicated airspeed left us high and fast on our first attempt so we initiated a go-around missed approach. There was a significant tailwind down the valley that sheared to a headwind at the surface this contributed to us being high and fast.While we were climbing out we were instructed to climb and maintain 15;000 feet and were given vectors back to TOCUD. Approaching TAKBE the Captain requested a turn direct to TAKBE from ATC. Being at 15;000 [feet] we couldn't lower the flaps [so] the Captain instructed me to set 12;200 [feet] for TAKBE and start down. I complied with these instructions and as we dropped below 15;000 [feet] we began lowering the flaps and configuring.Shortly after starting our descent ATC issued a low altitude alert and stated that his minimum vectoring altitude was 15;000 [feet]. We were visual with both the mountains and airport in sight but failed to get proper approval from ATC for the visual approach before descending. As a side note we were being shook pretty good by the continuous moderate turbulence and I was really having to work the thrust levers to maintain a safe airspeed. We informed ATC that we were visual and we were cleared for the approach to Runway 4. We successfully landed on our second attempt. column121: Early descent and low speed condition resulting in go-around. I was the Pilot Flying. Very short flight. Visual approach to RWY 15 at CHS. I was expecting the ILS approach. ATC recleared us direct to the airport and eventually direct MAMAE intersection to join the localizer for [Runway] 15 at 3;000 [feet] ft. Airport was in sight and we were cleared for a visual approach. I armed the approach and when we went into altitude capture at 3;000 [feet] I incorrectly set an altitude below 3;000 [feet] to allow the descent to continue in order to join the glide slope. I then realized we were not receiving the glide slope and were below the FAF crossing altitude at 1000ft. I disconnected the autopilot and stopped the descent. Unfortunately I did not also call for the flight directors off initially. I am relatively new to the equipment. Since we were in landing configuration of course the speed dropped rapidly. We were in landing configuration with the airport and PAPI's in sight but since the approach was unstable I decided to go around. We then flew the RWY 15 RNAV (GPS)Y to a normal landing. It was the third leg of a busy day with thunderstorm avoidance on the first two flights. It is my practice to carefully review the NOTAMs but somehow I missed the GS OTS. I haven't been into CHS as yet and the flight is very short and our ATC clearance had us high from the top of descent.Direct to a new airport on a time compressed flight for a visual at night is never in my opinion a pleasant way to conclude a long day of flying. Upon honest reflection I fully acknowledge I had a strong expectation bias for the ILS to 15. The lack of the GS and the unexpected consequences placed us in a reactionary position which is unacceptable.Our training is clear on how to capture and correct erroneous situations should they occur and we did our best to stop and correct an inadvertently entered unstable position. This was a clear example of the value and necessity of our human factors training. I know these things have happened before and I consider it my professional responsibility to not allow it to happen to me. And yet it did. Recognizing; and fully appreciating how higher than expected workload situations can present themselves is an essential aspect to our work. An increased diligence regarding the review of NOTAMs is a resounding suggestion I'm making to myself for one. Also; the need for particularly increased vigilance when in situations such as this is something I'll never forget.

Being distracted by the traffic close call; handling the radio swaps; and changing our approach I did not slow the aircraft down or add full flaps. Attempted to land with two notches of flaps and very fast; floated the aircraft most of the runway with braking in the final 1000 ft. Factors and Chain of Events:1. Long day of flying; and being tired from week at ZZZ1 contributed to wanting to be home. Additional time pressure of needing to pick up the family dog from the boarder affected decision making on speeds to fly and ultimately the runway selection.2. Concerns about forgetting to close the IFR flight plan; especially when tired; under time pressures; and distractions of passengers (kids); etc; contributed to cancelling in the air very close to the local airport operations. I should have stayed on the advisory frequency whenever within 5 miles of the airport that is known to be busy. Without ADS-B I would not have known about the departing traffic.3. Long two weeks of very good; challenging; and very safe flying supported an overconfidence in flying the airplane outside of SOPs; which contributed to flying way too fast on short final and almost floating the entire runway. Established patterns; speeds; altitudes; and power settings are practiced and used for good reason...to take variability out of flying and allow for handling of non-routine issues. Flying outside of SOP adds variability and multiplies risks that could overwhelm the pilot.4. Inaction of sticking with the originally stated plan to enter the downwind for Runway 31; the radio call is not just an advisory of what I am doing; but provides information to other operators on how the airport is flowing. Changing the plan adds risk to all of the other operators.
