column123: Vectored off ZZZZZ1 X just after ZZZZZ1 to follow traffic. Given a descent from FL170 down to 9000. Descended in FLC at 250kts. Turned back towards the southwest and given a descent to 7200 continued in FLC. Cleared direct to ZZZZZ and then cleared for the ILS XX. I selected direct ZZZZZ and engaged LNAV. I ask if everyone agreed that we could set 5100 for the ZZZZZ crossing and all agreed. 5100 was put in the MCP (Mode Control Panel) however; I failed to engage VNAV and we continue to descend in FLC. We leveled at 5100' about 15-20nm NE of ZZZZZ. The ATC comms became broken. I had Terrain selected on my MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) and was monitoring as I'm aware of terrain east of the airport. There were green depictions in the vicinity of ZZZZZ but none immediately near us. Nonetheless; I had the nagging feeling that something wasn't right. ATC was calling us; but their transmission was broken. We finally got a clear one asking us our altitude; at which time they told us to climb back to 7200 and maintain that to ZZZZZ (something they didn't verbalize with the initial approach clearance). Upon hearing that; I disengage the autopilot; pushed the thrust levers to the N1 bugs and immediately climbed to 7200. At that point; I engaged the autopilot; continued direct to ZZZZZ with the APP mode armed and flew an uneventful ILS XX to landing. To be clear; we did not have any GPWS terrain cautions or warnings throughout the descent; approach or landing.

column121: I was contracted to photograph the property at Location X.The property was at the lateral border of class D airspace over ZZZ [Airport]. That border cuts through the parking lot of the property I was photographing. My research in advance had showed the area as LAANC enabled for instant approval up to 400 feet; and only part of the potential operation zone was in restricted airspace. I didn't request that authorization in advance because I was conducting four flights across a 100 mile radius that day and didn't think I could accurately predict my arrival time.This was my fourth and last property of the day for this client; most of which were smaller portions of larger building complexes. The actual amount of land owned by the client at Location X ended up being much smaller than I had anticipated; and so was my operating zone. I picked my takeoff location and pulled up the Aloft air control app; which said that LAANC was not enabled for my operation. I misunderstood this to mean that my operation was outside of the zone requiring authorization as long as I stayed below the legal ceiling of 400 ft.I took off and conducted the flight; and halfway through I received a notification from DJI that I had entered a warning zone. I used the DJI map to navigate away from that area; take a few more shots outside of it; and land a few minutes later. I checked the Aloft map again after landing and realized that there was a temporary flight restriction in place for the entire class D zone around ZZZ; and that I had entered that zone for maybe 1-3 minutes.Primary cause is Pilot Error (Hazardous attitude; inexperience and misinterpretation of maps and restrictions)-The operation zone I discovered when I arrived differed somewhat from what I had researched and planned in advance. -I was licensed several years ago; but I've only conducted about 6-10 commercial flights since then; and none in controlled airspace until Day 0. I had submitted my first LAANC request in Location Y earlier that morning. I wasn't familiar with how the map displayed temporary flight restrictions; I failed to reference the legend; and I misread the situation.-I covered multiple properties in a 100-mile radius that day; and this was the last of the day; leaving me somewhat fatigued and impulsive. I should've rescheduled the property when I realized I was confused instead of proceeding with my best; most convenient guess.Secondary cause may be LAANC software ambiguity. The language for LAANC authorization not being available vs not being required is similar with the app I was using.This was my first experience with LAANC and I have enough first-hand knowledge of the procedure now to significantly reduce my confusion in the future. I won't hesitate to reschedule in the future if I can't be sure I'm in compliance.

column121: It was my take off out of ZZZ. Right as we were about to hit 100 knots or the high speed regime we got a master caution for and right side IRS (Inertial Reference System) fault. Captain said continue so I did. We rotated as normal. However as I started transitioning from flying visually to inside I looked down and realized I had the VERT HDG AND ATT flags as well as no flight director guidance. I glanced over and saw the captains instruments and flight director were there and working. Being a more critical phase of flight I didn't say anything to the captain yet due to not wanting to startle him more than necessary and I knew I could fly based of his instruments and visually. Once we got through 1000 ft and I knew we were safely away from the ground I stated that I didn't have any of that guidance. The captain said well let me take the plane and radios so you can run checklists to try to fix the issues. Once we transferred the controls I started looking through the non normals. I started by trying to look for any checklist relating to my instrumentation failure. I looked and read through display failure but we both stated this didn't make sense cuz the display was fine. After talking we said the first indication was the IRS FAULT light so let's start there. I started reading through that checklist and performing the actions it stated. It was around that time I realized we had performed a bleeds off TO and we hadn't switched the bleeds to the engines yet. So I performed that action before we got into any type of unsafe situation. Continuing that IRS FAULT checklist it had me turn the IRS selectors switch to both on left. As soon as I did that my side had all instrumentation and guidance once again. At this point we had leveled off at 270 because neither autopilot was working and they wouldn't let us into rvsm airspace without a working autopilot. I had sent a message to Maintenance Control stating our failures so that we could try to get the best guidance possible in trouble shooting. We transferred the controls back to me so he could talk to dispatch and manage the situation. Due to being 10000 ft lower than planned we weren't sure we would make it to ZZZ1. So we made a plan to go to ZZZ2 if needed based on how our fuel burn was going. We also made a plan to change controls back and forth so neither of us get too tired due to having to hand fly. We realized after a while we hadn't updated the cruise winds. Once we did that we realized we were right above bingo fuel. Then after flying a little while long we got below bingo so the decision was immediately made to go to ZZZ2. This entire time we were conferring with dispatch and they agreed. On the descent into ZZZ2 every time we started descending my vertical guidance went out on the flight director. So I again just used other instruments to back up my descent and every time we leveled off the vertical guidance came back on my flight director. Once we got on the approach both my vertical and lateral guidance went out. I was comfortable with flying it raw data and visually so continued flying to landing. Due to the added stress of everything that had gone on the entire flight and having to hand fly for over 4 hours by the time we got to the gate both of us felt somewhat fatigued and weren't sure if we really felt safe to continue. I talked to maintenance to add the failures on decent and approach to our list of failures we had already reported. While I did that captain called the chief pilot about everything and why we needed to do now. The manager asked how we felt and he said we are both on the fence. He went through the fatigue questions and he said based on those answers you guys aren't fit to fly and you are fatigued and will not continue. I don't think we did anything wrong on the flight in any way and I think we worked together well to divide or manage the workload. All of that added stress to flying and having to do so much more work than normal I know drained me which lead to me being fatigued.
column123: During the van ride to the airport; the FO and I reviewed the flight plan. The dispatcher notes included 'WILL NEED RWY XXL FOR TAKEOFF IF CALM WINDS OR WINDS FAVOR RWY XXL' and 'PLANNED BLEEDS OFF FOR T.O.' It was also noted in the release that the First Class Cabin outlets were inoperative. We mentioned the noise abatement as a possible reason for the opposite direction takeoff; or better weight/climb performance. Upon reaching the airport; we walked straight from security to the aircraft. Rather than stopping for coffee on the way to the aircraft; the FO decided to return to the terminal for coffee after stowing his bags on the aircraft. After briefing the flight attendants; to include the potential wait of an opposite direction departure and the First Class outlets; the FO had not yet returned to the aircraft. In the interest of time; I completed the entire initialization of the FMC; with the exception of requesting takeoff data. One of our ACARS messages had revealed a weight restriction; so despite the close proximity between the reserve and REMF (Remaining Fuel); I opted not to add additional fuel; and decided to wait until fueling was finished to request more accurate takeoff data. The FO returned with his coffee and then performed the walk-around. While on the walk-around; the gate agent brought down the reconciliation; and I briefed the passengers about today's flight. Upon returning; the FO began his preflight flow; and I went to the bathroom. When I got back; he then went to the bathroom. The flight attendants had completed their checks and were ready to close the cockpit door; but needed to wait until the FO was finished to do so. Once he returned to the flight deck; the door was closed. At this point; I realized that the autothrottle was not engaged; and so I checked the TAKEOFF page in the FMC and realized that neither of us had sent for the appropriate data yet. When asked; the FO stated that he had requested it; but our current weight was sending back an error for RWY XYR. As a result of his lack of initiative; I suggested that he send for numbers on XXL; as dispatch had requested. He did so; and it also returned an error for being overweight. The suggested value; was roughly 300lbs below our current weight; and due to the line of aircraft that had formed for a XYR departure; I was willing to accept this weight since our wait for an opposite direction departure would likely; burn enough fuel. He believed the weight for XYR was close; and so I permitted him to send it again. The required weight for a XYR departure was roughly 1000 pounds below that for a XXL departure. I told him to send for numbers at the maximum weights specified in the error; and if we got below the number for XYR before our opposite direction departure is permitted; we can do that. I also acknowledged that this weight would be extremely close to our required reserve fuel. Once he sent for a successful solution; I reviewed it and realized that the auto function for the bleed air was recommending a bleeds on solution. I then had him send for takeoff data forcing a bleeds off takeoff; at which point our current weight returned a valid solution for RWYXXR. We were past our scheduled departure time at this point; so we quickly briefed the departure; noting the threats of complacency from day-4; the bleeds off takeoff; and the line of aircraft we would be waiting in. Despite acknowledging these threats; I permitted the first error to be introduced by not requesting a more thorough brief of the clearance and SID; or verifying that the selected altitude was correct. It was not. 3000 feet was still selected from the arrival crew; despite our being cleared to climb via the SID; and the top altitude of the ZZZZZX being 13;000 feet.After completing the before push checklist; we notified the ground crew and pushed off the gate approximately 5 minutes late; and a line of approximately 8-10 aircraft had already formed. The ground crew advised us toturn on our lights; at which point the FO turned on two light switches. I did not verify which switches. During our taxi; the ground controller asked us to re-cycle our transponder. The FO had not turned on the transponder during push; and turned it on now. All checklists and callouts were accomplished satisfactorily through our clearance for takeoff on RWY XYR. During the takeoff roll; approaching 100 KIA; a Master Caution illuminated corresponding to an IRS (Inertial Reference System) annunciator. I extinguished it and verbalized continue; followed by the 100 knots; V1; and VR callouts. Once airborne; the FO directed me to retract the flaps and perform the after takeoff checklist. During final flap retraction; the FO verbalized that he had lost some of his displayed instrumentation. I assumed he meant his Flight Director; and opted to take the aircraft as my displays were operating normally. I continued to fly the departure and climb. Approaching 3000 feet; the Flight Director commanded a level off; as this was the altitude selected in the MCP (Mode Control Panel). I began decreasing power and leveling off as I recognized the VNAV ALT in the FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) and cross checked the MCP to deduce that this was not due to the departure. I grabbed the printed PDC and quickly located the clearance to climb via SID. I then resumed the climb noting the next 5000B restriction at ZZZZZ1. Due to the timing of this mistake; it resulted in neither pilot accomplishing the After Takeoff or No Engine Bleed Checklists. This small error that was not repaired during the briefing permitted additional errors to occur; contributing to a lower fuel state.As we continued the climb; the FO continued to troubleshoot his displays and I eventually became aware that in addition to losing the Flight Director (FD); the FO's ADI and HSI were black; with yellow ATT; HDG; and VERT annunciations; but accurate speed and altitude was still displayed. He began searching for a non-normal checklist associated with the malfunctioning display. At this point; I opted to take the radios in addition to flying the aircraft. Passing 10;000 feet I switched the sterile light; 'double dinged' the flight attendants; checked and verbalized that the cabin was pressurizing; and attempted to turn on the autopilot. However; the sterile light was apparently in the wrong position; so instead of turning it off; I inadvertently turned it on. I typically engage the autopilot at this time; but it failed to engage on either the A or B channel. I cycled the FO's FD switch; to make my source the master; and attempted to engage the autopilot again. It did not engage; so I continued to hand fly the aircraft. To prevent myself from overwhelming the FO; who was still searching for an appropriate checklist; I decided not to inform him that the autopilot was not functioning until it became pertinent. The FO reviewed several non-normal checklists and we deduced that they were not the correct checklists. At one point; the Flight Attendants called the flight deck. The FO took the call; as I had my hands full. They were asking why the sterile light had been turned on; and he notified them of our predicament; and I turned the light back off. This was the consequence of yet another error that was not repaired on the ground; adding additional complication to this situation. The flight attendants also informed us that in addition to the outlets being inoperative in the First Class Cabin; they were inoperative in the entire aircraft; all of the screens at the seats were inoperative; and there was no internet connectivity. During this time we passed FL180; and set 29.92 inHg at which point I chimed in that it is possible to use one of the reversionary switches to simply force my display onto his. In reviewing the overhead panel; the FO discovered that the bleed air was not appropriately set. He quickly performed the procedure to set the bleed panel without referencing the No Engine Bleed Checklist. He then set the gear; auto-brakes; and igniters to complete the After Takeoff Checklist. Thankfully the APU was still pressurizing the cabin despite being above 17;000 feet; and maintaining an approximately 5;000 foot cabin altitude. Although we repaired this error before it became an undesired aircraft state; we simultaneously introduced another error as the appropriate checklist was the No Engine Bleed Checklist. Therefore; the APU continued running.Returning his attention to the overhead panel; I attempted to help guide him to the appropriate switch while keeping my eyes on the gauges because I was hand-flying. I then mentioned that there are also reversionary switches on the dash; and perhaps it was one of those. He did move several of these switches but only the upper and lower DU'S (Display Units) changed; so he returned to the overhead. He eventually actuated several of those switches; and again got no positive resolution. As a result; I guided him back to the original indication - the IRS Master Caution. On the overhead panel; the R IRS FAULT and ALIGN lights were illuminated. He located the IRS FAULT checklist. During the climb; ATC eventually cleared us to an RVSM altitude. Knowing that autopilot is a required piece of equipment; I declined that altitude and was cleared to FL270. At this point; I filled in the FO that the autopilot was not functioning. After performing the checklist steps; the FO's instrumentation was restored; but the autopilot still would not engage; and the #2 transponder displayed a fault; so the #1 was selected. We interfaced with Maintenance Control via ACARS for any additional assistance. With the FO's display functioning correctly; I asked if he felt good enough to fly. He confirmed that he was; and I handed aircraft control over to him. We agreed to trading off who would fly every 30-60 minutes to avoid fatigue. At this point; I started my timer and began interfacing with dispatch about our options. This included requesting to transit RVSM airspace as a non-RVSM capable aircraft; which was denied multiple times. While at cruise in ZZZ Center's airspace; we discussed divert options with dispatch and opted to continue as the FMC computed FOB at ZZZ1 was 5.7; which was above the required 5.5. I also sent multiple ELB (Electronic Logbook) reports for the various issues we encountered. We also discussed the possibility that this was a larger electrical malfunction; as opposed to simply an IRS FAULT. I then realized that I had not requested new winds for our lower altitude. After doing so; our calculated FOB decreased. However; dispatch revised the alternate which decreased the required fuel to 5.1; which we were above. As a result of some storms in the area; we needed to use the Engine Anti-Ice; again decreasing our FOB calculation; now below the required 5.1. Shortly thereafter; the center tanks were emptied; the center fuel pumps were turned off; and dispatch notified us that an alternate was no longer required. The required fuel was now 4.4; and the FMC calculated to have 4.7 FOB at ZZZ1; so we continued. As a result of the inadvertent APU usage; the use of ENG ANTI-ICE at cruise; the variations associated with hand flying; and common fuel system anomaly associated with a decreasing FOB after turning off the center fuel pumps; our fuel total slowly decreased below the 4.4 FOB requirement. At this point; the decision was made to divert to ZZZ2. During our descent; the FO's instrumentation began further degrading. During descents in VNAV; LVL CHG; and V/S; the FO would lose his vertical Flight Director; but it would reappear at the level off altitude. I offered to fly as my display was functioning correctly; and he declined. I made sure to keep an eye on our flight path; and the FO was doing a great job without my interference. We were cleared to fly the visual approach to RWYXZR at ZZZ; and backed it up with the ILS. We discussed the possibility of his Flight Director malf

column121: Working combined positions as normal this early in the morning. Slightly more complex because of lower weather in ZZZ1 area but nothing too bad. Aircraft X was 1 of three aircraft being sequenced with the third being a flight school who had already requested an unusual pop up IFR and had been difficult to deal with. There was icing for the departures from ZZZ as well which the Aircraft X had experienced earlier adding  a bit of complexity. Again; nothing too unusual. The previous days had been bad thunderstorm days and I was working multiple extreme complexity sessions with metering to ZZZ and already was feeling pretty beat down and tired  by the week but was powering through. Aircraft X was set up on approach; read back correct. It was a 'T' shaped RNAV approach. I noticed almost immediately that he blew through the turn to final; but just barely and looked to be correcting which he said he was when questioned. At this point he's a few hundred feet below the Minimum IFR Altitude (MIA) but has been established and cleared on a segment of the approach and had been following the routing and altitudes fine.Shortly thereafter I realized his correction was wrong; he was well below my MIA as he was following altitude guidance on approach but obviously had 'slopped'/missed the turn to final and I issued the first low altitude alert. Aircraft X seemed confused and he asked 'was that for me?' to which I replied 'yes; low altitude alert; Aircraft X climb and maintain 080 immediately; approach clearance cancelled' he then began his climb. I showed him about a mile and a half south of approach course that he thought he was on. I then had to re-sequence the aircraft to make Aircraft X last. I was working multiple departures out of ZZZ while this was happening. Once getting him level at 080; I asked him about being off course. He said something about the GPS being weird at the turn to final; asked for the approach straight in. I told him he had to be resequenced which I started to work on. Feeling completely unlucky and beat down I told the Supervisor 'i need to get off position now' which could have been accomplished by breaking training that was on the adjacent scope D side that had no traffic. But they opted to let me sit there and wait for someone who was coming back from break in the next 5 minutes. So; I continued to work planes under stress and duress.Overall; I had already thought that there had been a lot of unprepared and unprofessional pilots this morning with the unexpected lower weather condition in ZZZ1 area. Was asked for visuals when ceiling was overcast 026. people filed to satellite airports with no approaches. Aircraft asking for inactive runways; approaches that are out of service etc. Pop up IFR's immediately after take off. Pilots are not preparing properly. Furthermore; taking action to get a controller off position imminently when they ask needs to be a priority of any means possible following an incident. Sure this wasn't the worst/most imminent incident but if a controller is saying they need off to clear their head; it is a safety issue for management to not take immediate action to address that.

column121: Around XA:30 on Day 1; while conducting traffic pattern work; a student and I were cleared to take off on XXR and told to make right closed traffic. I did not catch the ATC instruction to 'follow traffic;' only the takeoff clearance and right traffic instruction. In the upwind and upon reaching 700 feet; the student began a right turn. Immediately upon rolling onto the crosswind; we gained sight of traffic on the downwind at the same time ATC called to asked if we had the downwind traffic in sight. I immediately took the flight controls and made a left turn towards the upwind to avoid traffic and reported traffic in sight. I continued in the upwind until ATC advised to turn right and enter the downwind; follow traffic and advise the traffic in sight. We reported the downwind traffic in sight; made a right turn into the downwind to rejoin. On the downwind; we were cleared to land on XXR. After landing; we taxied back to the ramp; shut down and debriefed. I debriefed the situation with the student and made sure to emphasize the importance of maintaining vigilance in the traffic pattern and scanning for traffic. I made it known that I wasn't upset with them and that it was a huge lesson for me and for the student as well. As an instructor; I am trusted to stay vigilant; pay full attention to every radio call and ask ATC for clarification if unsure. I have done a lot of reflecting on this occurrence and went back and listened to the ATC audio recording to figure out how all of this happened. I was pretty shaken up afterwards and still keep asking myself 'How can a 1;000 hour pilot let something like that occur?' I believe a large contributing factor to this incident was fatigue and inadequete nutrition and hydration. I had spent the entire day before (Day 0) volunteering for a non-profit as a pilot. That day had been long and involved extensive waiting on the ground for thunderstorms with insufficient food and water. I believe that had lingering effects on me that night and into the next day (the day of the occurrence). I woke up the next morning feeling a little tired; but thought I felt well enough to fly and work. Feeling rushed that morning; I also did not pack a lunch that morning like I normally do. I refilled my water once that day; but I don't think I was drinking enough. Knowing it was a 90 degree day and I had multiple activities scheduled; I should have taken extra care to hydrate and make sure I was getting enough food. Over all this occurrence has been very eye-opening for me and has taught me huge lessons. One is the paramount importance of remaining vigilant during traffic pattern instructional flights. The other is the importance of checking myself with the IMSAFE checklist that we all preach. It is hugely apparent that the consequences of not doing so can potentially be deadly! I take full responsibility and realize the seriousness of the situation. I wish to use this as a learning moment for myself and my student. Moving forward; I plan to take at an absolute minimum 1 day off of flying completely every week so that I can rest and ensure I am completely present for each and every flight operation and prevent anything like this from ever reoccuring.

column121: The ongoing prohibition of parallel visual approaches at the San Francisco Airport has escalated from an operational inconvenience to a critical safety hazard. The resulting daily Ground Delay Programs (GDP) introduce two unmitigated risks into our system: chronic flight crew fatigue and unpredictable; near-minimum fuel operations.The SFO GDP frequently spans to XA:00 to XQ:00; causing domestic delays ranging from 45 to over 90 minutes. This systematically pushes flight crews to the limits of their Flight Duty Period (FDP); transforming a standard 8 to 10 hour duty day into exhausting 10 to 12 hour marathons. Pilots are regularly forced to fly complex arrivals into a high-density environment after being delayed - sometimes for multiple hours - where fatigue becomes a major factor.This threat materialized on day two of our pairing. Our schedule consisted of a three leg sequence: ZZZZ - SFO; SFO - ZZZZ; and a return to SFO. Both segments into SFO were hit by GDP delays exceeding one hour. The second GDP would have pushed us past our legal 13-hour FDP limit. While the crew desk was able to proactively remove us from the final turn - at considerable financial cost and inconvenience to our customers - many other crews had not timed out. Instead; they are being forced to fly into SFO fatigued; having already exhausted their mental and physical reserves waiting out ground delays.The current SFO configuration also severely compromises fuel planning predictability. Because a GDP of over an hour does not guarantee a clear path upon arrival; clear weather (CAVOK) days now yielding traffic saturation risks usually reserved for low-visibility operations.The severity of this breakdown was demonstrated on our flight from ZZZZ to SFO. The weather at SFO was pristine; endless blue skies with standard westerly winds. Normally; a remaining fuel of 1 hour 15 minutes is sufficient fuel to conduct an approach; handle a go-around; and land with a comfortable 60-minute reserve. Recognizing the SFO volatility; we planned a conservative gate fuel giving us an increased remaining fuel of 1 hour 45 minutes.The fuel preservation effort began immediately on the ground in ZZZZ; where our wheels-up time meant a 15-minute wait at the runway end. We proactively taxied on one engine and shut down the motor during our wait to preserve our margins. However; as we approached SFO our situation deteriorated. While on the BDEGA Arrival; ZOA assigned us a published hold at BGGLO due to traffic saturation on the SFO final approach.We immediately slowed the aircraft and began coordinating our fuel status with dispatch. I determined a bingo fuel of approximately 7;500 lb. before we needed to divert to SMF (1 hour remaining fuel of 5;100 lb. plus 2;300 lb. burn to SMF). We entered the BGGLO hold at 8;900 lb. After just one circuit our fuel had dropped to 8;300 lbs. Recognizing that a third circuit would push us below our diversion threshold; I informed ZOA that the second lap would have to be our final circuit; we either needed to press to SFO or immediately divert to SMF.Fortunately; ZOA released us from the hold with 7;700 lb. remaining. This left us with almost no buffer. To maintain a safe margin at SFO; I wanted a minimum touchdown fuel of 6;300 lb. (1 hour remain fuel of 5;100 lb. plus 1;200 burn to SJC allowing for a go-around at SFO and a diversion to SJC with a 45-minute reserve). I was mentally prepared to declare minimum fuel" and even "emergency fuel" to NORCAL Approach if given any further delay vectors; as the low-speed and low-altitude small box patterns frequently used by ATC during these saturation periods consume fuel at an accelerated rate. I realize 6;300 lb. remaining fuel is higher than Company policy. However I never want to box myself into a position where a go-around will result in an unsafe fuel state.NORCAL managed to sequence us with minimal vectoring; and we landed at SFO with 6;500 lb. While safe; this was significantly belowour flight-planned remaining fuel of 8;281 lb.Despite departing ZZZZ with an extra 30 minutes of fuel on a perfect clear-weather day; the compounding ground and airborne delays brought us to within minutes of an unnecessary diversion. The current SFO arrival restrictions are creating a compound hazard: crews are being kept in the air longer resulting in increasingly narrower fuel margins; all while operating at the tail end of extended and fatigue-inducing duty days. The FAA MUST re-evaluate the prohibition on parallel visuals to restore system predictability and preserve safety margins."

column121: Our facility is understaffed. We are allowed 12; 14 with training. We have 9; with 1 controller medically disqualified since the start of the busy season. Day 0 is the final day of the busy season. All our controllers are burned out. Everyone has been doing 6 day work weeks; lots of 10 hour days. Additionally in an attempt to get more staffing; our manager has increased our required time on position and reduced break times and lunch breaks. Moral of the story; we are burnt out. I had been fighting a cold or sickness of some sort and am not 100% at this time. I'm tired; I'm sick. I'm now in my 9th or 10th hour of work. The airport had an event on Day 0. There were several aircraft participating. Before the event; the aircraft altogether did about 100 separate ops in the traffic pattern; wearing out my supervisor and I; the only two there that morning. Luckily a third; fresh controller worked the event itself when he arrived to work at XA:15.During the event; all ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) units staged at Location X; which is across the airfield from the fire station. After the event was over; they called to relocate back to the fire station; needing to cross both parallel runways. My supervisor was working LC; at my request; as I was just so worn out and could barely talk or think anymore; that I felt I would only be safe on ground control; if that. So ARFF calls me and requests to cross both runways back to the fire station. At this time; Aircraft X is lining up to depart rwy XXL. I coordinate a conditional crossing reference the departing aircraft. My SUP approves the conditional.'ARFF and company; CROSS runway XX right at 1. HOLD SHORT runway XX left at 1.'I receive a perfect readback. I watch very carefully as the 3 ARFF units cross XXR. They get to the other side (Taxiway 2) and come to a full stop after clearing the runway. I literally nod my head and say to myself; that's what I want to see. I turn to watch this beautiful aircraft depart XXL and to know when it has passed Taxiway 1 so I can cross the ARFF units. Looks good; roaring down the runway. I make one last check on the ARFF units and turn my head toward them one more time. As my eyes see ARFF; I observe them moving fast (25-40 mph) across TWY 2. I key up the frequency and pretty much yell; 'ARFF; STOP!!!' The lead fire truck slams on it's breaks. I watch as the truck tips forward in its best attempt to stop. The other trucks also stop. ARF is over the hold short line. Seeing that they have all come to a complete stop; I quickly glance over to the aircraft to see if there is any way to cancel take off clearance. It is just airborne between taxiways 3 and 1. At this point; it was safer to let them takeoff. I clutch my chest because I literally can't fathom the thought of what had almost just occurred.The aircraft has now passed and I give the ARFF units clearance to cross runway XXL. I got off position quickly thereafter and left for the day.Recommendation: All of our controllers have had negative experiences with ARFF and how many mistakes on the airfield they have made. I love fire fighters; but these guys (and gals) need more training. The controller's have talked about having them over to the tower and giving them classes during our slow period; but it never seems to happen. Given incidents like this; perhaps the FAA can mandate some driver's tests or something for ARFF on the airfield.Nothing follows.

column121: At the time of the event; the flight crew had been awake for more than 24 hours; having flown over 5 hours; and were completing the final leg of a demanding red-eye trip. Extreme fatigue was a significant compounding factor. Furthermore; as a low-time pilot in type (100 hours); I had not received extensive or standardized training regarding the specific nuances and verification sequence of the Aircraft X parking brake system.Sequence of Events:The aircraft was parked on an inclined ramp with the engines shut down; parking brake disengaged; and chocks in place. The Captain instructed me to set the parking brake. I pulled the parking brake handle; but did not visually verify hydraulic accumulator pressure or the corresponding brake indicator light status. The Captain observed the physical handle position but did not cross-check the system pressure before exiting the aircraft to remove the chocks. No chocks were left behind the wheels to act as a secondary barrier.After re-entering the cabin to secure the cargo door and net; the aircraft began rolling backward due to the incline. Because I was performing pre-flight duties for the next leg and the Captain was focused on the cargo area; the initial movement went unnoticed.Upon realizing the aircraft was moving; I immediately applied the toe brakes; but no braking action was achieved due to a lack of system hydraulic pressure. Ground crew began alerting us to the movement. The Captain hurried to the left seat and also applied the toe brakes with no effect. I attempted to assist by applying passenger-side toe brakes and verbally asked the Captain if I should cycle the parking brake handle forward; I received no response due to the high-stress environment. The Captain subsequently activated the standby hydraulic pump and utilized the steering tiller to steer the aircraft away from immediate hazards; but the aircraft ultimately collided with a parked airframe before coming to a complete stop.Lessons Learned / Safety Recommendations:This incident underscores the critical danger of severe crew fatigue on decision-making and cross-checking procedures. To prevent future occurrences; the exact sequential verification of the parking brake system--including verifying accumulator pressure and indicator lights--must be explicitly taught in training and verified via a mandatory checklist item before chocks are pulled. Reliance on physical handle position alone creates an unsafe latent error.

column121: The FO was PF; I was PM. Normal pushback; taxi out. All checklists ran; no abnormal indications. Applied takeoff power. FO rotated (noticed a momentary pause in his positive rate; gear up" call); climbing through roughly 200-300ft; Master Caution for FLT CONT; I looked up and noticed no less than 5 orange lights illuminated. STBY RUDDER; SYS A Low Pressure; 1-2 in that top let panel portion that I can't recall; and bottom right on the Hydraulic panel; both HYD A ENG and ELEC LOW PRESS lights on. I immediately when to the SYS synoptic page to check quantity and pressure. Quantity was full; A was showing 106. B normal. A pressure was rapidly dropping and I saw it bottom at around 400PSI for about 15 seconds. The it slowly came up up. At this point I told the FO to continue flying the airplane; I told ATC; who at this point just handed us off to ZZZ DEP; that we would need to remain at 4000; and stay in the local area. They acknowledged this. At this point I begin to investigate the issue. Quantity was good; pressure on the A side was still low. All lights were extinguished except HYD A ENG. At this point I asked the FO "did you see all the lights"; at which point he said he felt very heavy controls on rotation and "had to pull the airplane off the ground." I went into the FOM non-normals in the iPad and went to Loss of HYD A. The condition is 3 illuminated lights-- all of which were illuminated at one point; and currently just HYD A ENG was still. The FO and I had a quick discussion that this checklist was the safest and most prudent checklist to run. So I began. Completed in it's entirety until it called for the manual gear extension. At this point ATC had cleared us to climb to 6000; and enter a present position hold. The checklist drove us to secure HYD A; and given it's depth; and the condition of the airplane and the FO's input about heavy controls; I both agreed requesting priority handling and returning to ZZZ was the SAFEST path. 175 SOB's and 90 minutes of fuel was relayed to ATC/ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting). Checklist complete; FA's briefed with standard items; PAX's notified of the issue and return to ZZZ; and Dispatch was notified of the priority handling and return. I disconnected wi-fi after the priority handling request and PAX notified. We left the hold and asked for vectors to XXR (longest of the two). The cleared us to join at a 7 mile final. On the dog legged I manually extended the gear and ran the deferred landing checklist. The FO performed the landing; we landed safely and exited the runway and taxied to gate XX under our own power."
column123: I was the PF and everything was normal up to the ROTATE command. The force to rotate the airplane was much heavier than normal. These actions caused a delay in my call for POSITIVE RATE/GEAR UP. Climbing through 200ft agl the captain mentioned the illuminated lights we had in regards to the A hydraulic system. I assumed that aircraft would give way to us. As I crossed XY; I saw the aircraft began to turn toward us like they were getting onto Taxiway 5 heading northwest-bound. At first; I still thought they would give way. As our nose crossed the north runway edge line of runway XY. It became obvious that the aircraft was not going to give way. The FO said 'watch out for that guy.' I applied the brakes and came to a stop. After we stopped; ZZZ ground told us to give way to the aircraft. I Turned off the landing lights; runway turnoff lights; and taxi light. Both the FO and I were shocked that our taxi instructions would have caused a collision. If I did not take the initiative to stop; but instead followed the taxi clearance; there would have been a collision. The FO told ZZZ ground that this situation was 'poorly coordinated.' ZZZ ground acknowledged that by mumbling. It was an unsatisfying response from ZZZ ground. We taxied to the gate and parked. During deplaning; I asked the flight attendant if they noticed an abnormal brake application during the taxi in and they said yes.Cause: Threats present were nighttime operations; a runway crossing; thunderstorms and rain in the area; a long duty day; and poor coordination between ZZZ tower; ground; our flight; and the other aircraft. I am curious to know why the aircraft decided to turn in front of us when we were moving 14 kt ground speed with all of our lights illuminated and exiting a runway.

column123: Sample synopsesWe were conducting a initial training flight. This was the X leg of the day. We were returning from ZZZ to ZZZ1.  We were above maximum landing weight and decided to shoot an approach to EEN.  The upgrade pilot conducted a thorough briefing for the localizer runway 02 with a circle to a planned low approach to runway 20.  The approach; circle and low approach were uneventful.  We were monitoring the CTA frequency for EEN; and made the appropriate 10 mile; 5 mile; initiating circle; and turning final radio calls.  We did not hear any traffic in the pattern; see any traffic in the traffic pattern; or note any traffic on the TCAS.  The upgrade pilot conducted a rejected landing in accordance with the brief and initiated a VFR departure from runway 20 at EEN.  Because the pattern was clear; I injected a simulated dual engine flame out during departure.  The upgrade pilot initiated an emergency return to runway 02; lowered the landing gear; made the appropriate radio calls; flew a visual approach to runway 02 and then initiated a rejected landing to runway 02 due to aircraft weight being above maximum landing weight.  During climb out; we visually identified Aircraft X on final for runway 20 and subsequently received a TCAS traffic advisory call.  Since we had visually seen Aircraft X had already initiated a climb out; no evasive actions were required. We passed well above and to the right of Aircraft X's flight path. We made our departure radio calls and continued our departure. During the debrief; we attempted to determine why we were unaware of Aircraft X on final for runway 20.  We were able to talk with the crew of Aircraft X and discussed the event.  They stated they had been talking with Boston Center and that they too had been making radio calls on CTAF.  They stated that they had not heard any of our radio calls; but had visually seen us during our circling maneuver. However; they subsequently lost visual of us when we departed to the south and did not pick us up again until we had passed above into the right of their location while on file for runway 20.  Between the two crews; we identified the root cause of the situation as a lack of radio communication. However; we are unable to determine why the two aircraft were unable to hear each other's radio calls.  The most likely cause was an improperly tuned radio; however; both crews recall being on the proper frequency.  This ultimately degraded the situational awareness for both crews.Another root causes the lack of visual identification of other aircraft in the traffic pattern.  Although we had scanned the area for aircraft; both visually and on the TCAS; we did not see Aircraft X.  The Aircraft X crew had visually acquired us and was maintaining visual separation however; they lost this once we initiated a low approach and departed to the south.For our aircraft; this was the X leg of the day. We were approaching six hours of flight instruction and we had conducted multiple instrument approaches and landings; simulated emergencies; and VFR maneuvers.  Both the upgrade pilot and I were starting to get fatigued.  We communicated that to each other; and had elected to continue with the last few training events in order to get back on track due to days of weather canceled flights.  Another significant human factor is unfamiliarity with the local training environment. Neither the upgrade pilot nor I live in this area.  The upgrade pilot has flown in this area several times; but it is not a place that he operates routinely.  This was my first time flying in this area; so I was spending a significant amount of time ensuring that we remain clear of airspace and busy traffic patterns while we conducted our training.  We had flown several approaches at EEN during the second leg of training; so I was moderately familiar with the airport and surrounding airspace and had noted the high volume of a student pilot training at EEN particularly late morning and earlyafternoon.  I did find it unusual that there were no aircraft operating in the vicinity of EEN but I realized and assumed that most flight schools had ended operations for the day.During the debrief; the upgrade pilot and I discussed mitigation measures for future authorities at local non-towered airports.  Although the upgrade pilot is working on his type single pilot certification; we decided that it would be more appropriate if we created a challenge and response checklist for Non-Towered Airports (NTA).  For example; confirming that we are on the appropriate radio frequency; confirming that we are flying approaches to runways favored by wins; and actively confirming the number in location of aircraft in the NTA traffic pattern.  How the challenge and response does not normally occur during single pilot operations; we felt that it was appropriate to make that change in order to reduce the likelihood of a future incident on subsequent flights.  Additionally; we felt that it may improve safety during single pilot operations by having the pilot challenge and response themselves.

column121: I was acting as Second-in-Command during a southbound water landing in Part 135 seaplane operations.During the landing setup; the crew encountered increased workload due to an early duty day; expedited routing from ZZZ Tower; and river traffic. I selected a landing area on the right side of the river that had limited usable water due to ferries; small craft; and a helicopter.During descent; I made several power and pitch adjustments to prepare for landing. The aircraft responded more aggressively than expected; resulting in a higher-than-intended sink rate. I added power to arrest the sink; but the aircraft did not respond as anticipated. We contacted the top of a wave at approximately 59-60 knots; resulting in a bounce.I attempted a go-around; which was not appropriate for the aircraft's low speed and high pitch attitude. Additional power inputs resulted in a nose-high attitude; a power-on stall; and a tail strike. The aircraft remained controllable; and we taxied to a marina without further issues. No injuries occurred.Subsequent inspection revealed structural damage to the tail; including multiple bulkheads requiring replacement. I am committed to applying these lessons to prevent recurrence.
